summary: The instructions turn from animals to meal offerings made from grain, oil, and frankincense. Whether the grain is offered as flour, baked food, or fresh first fruits, a memorial portion is burned and the remainder ordinarily becomes the priests' most holy share.
whyItMatters: This chapter broadens the opening collection of offerings and shows how ordinary agricultural produce enters the sanctuary's ordered pattern of gift, memorial, and priestly portion.

context.author: The chapter continues the instructions presented as Yahweh's speech through Moses; it does not name the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: Israelites bringing meal offerings and Aaron's sons, who present the memorial portion and receive what remains.
context.date: The narrative setting is Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: The altar and priestly court of the Tent of Meeting, where grain offerings are presented within the book’s opening collection of offerings.
context.literaryForm: Ritual instruction organized by preparation method, followed by ingredient rules and a first-fruits case.

outline.heading: Fine flour, oil, and frankincense
outline.note: A handful becomes the altar's memorial portion, while the remainder belongs to the priests.

outline.heading: Baked, griddled, or pan-cooked offerings
outline.note: Several prepared forms follow the same division between a burned memorial and a priestly portion.

outline.heading: Yeast, honey, and covenant salt
outline.note: The chapter excludes yeast and honey from altar fire and requires salt with every meal offering.

outline.heading: Fresh grain as first fruits
outline.note: Parched and crushed fresh grain receives oil and frankincense before its memorial portion is burned.

keyVerses.text: He shall bring it to Aaron’s sons, the priests. He shall take his handful of its fine flour, and of its oil, with all its frankincense, and the priest shall burn its memorial on the altar, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This sentence introduces the memorial portion, the priest's action, and the offering's altar destination.

keyVerses.text: That which is left of the meal offering shall be Aaron’s and his sons’. It is a most holy part of the offerings of Yahweh made by fire.
keyVerses.why: The repeated rule shows that the unburned remainder is an assigned priestly portion, not discarded material.

keyVerses.text: Every offering of your meal offering you shall season with salt. You shall not allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be lacking from your meal offering. With all your offerings you shall offer salt.
keyVerses.why: The chapter gives salt a covenant association and makes it mandatory across meal offerings.

questions.question: What is a meal offering if no meal is described?
questions.answer: In this chapter it is a grain offering made as fine flour, baked cakes or wafers, food prepared on a griddle or pan, or fresh parched grain. Oil accompanies every form, and frankincense accompanies the flour and first-fruits forms.

questions.question: What is the memorial portion?
questions.answer: It is the part the priest removes from the offering and burns on the altar. The chapter calls it a memorial but does not explain the term further; the repeated contrast is between this burned portion and the remainder given to the priests.

questions.question: Why do Aaron and his sons receive most of the offering?
questions.answer: The chapter repeatedly assigns the remainder to the priests and labels it most holy. It presents this as their designated share of the offerings made by fire, without giving a separate economic or symbolic explanation here.

questions.question: Why are yeast and honey barred from the altar fire?
questions.answer: Verses 11-12 state the boundary but do not state its rationale. They prohibit burning yeast or honey as an offering made by fire while still allowing them to be brought as first fruits, so explanations based on spoilage, health, or symbolism should not be treated as the chapter's own answer.

questions.question: What does “salt of the covenant” mean?
questions.answer: Verse 13 links salt with God's covenant and requires it with every meal offering. The chapter does not unpack the image, so it is clear that salt marks covenantal offering here even though the precise symbolism remains unstated.

questions.question: Do the different cooking methods create different kinds of offering?
questions.answer: Oven-baked, griddled, and pan-cooked preparations receive separate instructions, but each is still called a meal offering. Each uses fine flour and oil, and each comes to the priest and altar under the same memorial-and-remainder pattern.

questions.question: How does the first-fruits offering differ from the earlier cases?
questions.answer: It begins with fresh heads of grain that are parched and crushed rather than flour or prepared bread. Oil and frankincense are added, and the priest burns part of the grain, oil, and all the frankincense as its memorial portion.

questions.question: Does this chapter treat the grain offering as ordinary food?
questions.answer: No. The chapter calls its burned memorial a pleasant aroma to Yahweh and twice describes the priestly remainder as a most holy part of Yahweh’s offerings made by fire, with handling assigned to the priests.

glossary.def: A grain-based offering prepared from flour or fresh grain with oil, sometimes baked before presentation.
The selected part of a grain offering that the priest burns on the altar, distinguished from the priestly remainder.
Produce from the beginning of a harvest presented to God; here it may take the form of fresh parched grain.
An aromatic resin placed on the flour or fresh-grain offering and burned with its memorial portion.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The first chapter describes whole burnt offerings from herd, flock, and birds, including the offerer’s and priests’ duties.

here.text: Grain may be offered as flour, baked food, or fresh first fruits. A memorial portion burns on the altar, the remainder in the flour and cooked cases belongs to the priests, and the chapter regulates yeast, honey, and salt.

after.text: The next offering is a peace offering from herd or flock, with blood applied at the altar and specified fat reserved for burning.
